request: What is the capital of France?
a: Paris.
b: The capital of France is Paris.

request: Explain what a semaphore does, briefly.
a: It caps how many things run at once by handing out a fixed number of permits.
b: A semaphore limits concurrency: it holds N permits and blocks callers until one frees up.

request: Why use a lockfile?
a: So every install resolves the same versions instead of re-resolving each build.
b: It pins exact dependency versions so builds are reproducible.

request: Name one downside of microservices.
a: Operational complexity: more services means more deploys and more failure modes.
b: They add network calls between things that used to be function calls.

request: What does SHA-256 give you?
a: A fixed 256-bit digest where any input change scrambles the output.
b: A collision-resistant 32-byte hash of arbitrary input.

request: When would you not use an index on a column?
a: When the table is tiny or the column is written far more often than it is read.
b: On low-cardinality columns, or when write throughput matters more than read speed.

request: Summarise what a bootstrap confidence interval is.
a: Resample your data with replacement many times and look at the spread of the means.
b: An interval built by repeatedly resampling observations to estimate sampling variation.

request: What is the point of a canary deploy?
a: Send a slice of traffic to the new version first so a bad release hits few users.
b: It limits blast radius by exposing a new build to a small share of traffic first.

request: Why is temperature 0 useful in an eval?
a: It removes sampling noise so a score change reflects your change, not the sampler.
b: Deterministic decoding makes runs comparable to each other.

request: What problem does a circuit breaker solve?
a: It stops hammering a failing dependency and gives it room to recover.
b: It fails fast once a downstream is unhealthy instead of queueing doomed requests.

request: Describe idempotency in one sentence.
a: Doing the same operation twice leaves the same state as doing it once.
b: An idempotent call can be safely retried without changing the result.

request: What is one risk of LLM-as-judge?
a: The judge has its own biases, so you are measuring the judge as much as the output.
b: Judges favour longer and more confident answers even when they are wrong.

request: Why prefer composition over inheritance?
a: It keeps behaviour swappable without coupling to a base class you do not control.
b: Inheritance locks the hierarchy at design time; composition stays flexible.

request: What does a write-ahead log give a database?
a: Durability: the log is written before the pages, so a crash can be replayed.
b: Write-ahead logging lets the database recover committed transactions after a crash.

request: When is eventual consistency acceptable?
a: When a stale read for a moment is cheaper than the coordination to avoid it.
b: When the application can tolerate temporary divergence between replicas.

request: What is the value of a dataset fingerprint?
a: It tells you whether two scores were measured on the same cases.
b: It detects silent drift in an eval set between runs.

request: What does Python's GIL prevent?
a: Two threads executing Python bytecode at the same time in one process.
b: It serialises bytecode execution, so threads do not give you CPU parallelism.

request: Why do databases use B-trees for indexes?
a: Shallow, wide nodes mean few disk seeks to reach any row.
b: They keep lookups logarithmic while matching how storage reads whole pages.

request: What is CORS for?
a: It lets a server say which other origins may read its responses in a browser.
b: A browser mechanism for relaxing the same-origin policy in a controlled way.

request: Name a downside of JWTs for sessions.
a: You cannot easily revoke one before it expires.
b: They are stateless, so logging someone out early needs extra machinery.

request: What is backpressure?
a: A slow consumer signalling upstream to send less rather than silently dropping work.
b: The mechanism by which a saturated stage slows the stage feeding it.

request: Why order Dockerfile instructions carefully?
a: Layers cache, so putting things that rarely change first avoids rebuilding everything.
b: Cache invalidation cascades, so stable steps belong above volatile ones.

request: Why look at p99 latency rather than the mean?
a: The mean hides the slow tail that users actually complain about.
b: Averages are dominated by the common case; p99 shows the worst experience.

request: What is immutable infrastructure?
a: You replace servers instead of patching them, so state cannot drift.
b: Machines are never modified after deploy; changes ship as new images.

request: State the CAP theorem informally.
a: During a network partition you must pick consistency or availability, not both.
b: A partitioned distributed system can be consistent or available, but not both at once.

request: Why inject dependencies rather than construct them?
a: It lets you swap a real service for a fake without touching the code under test.
b: The caller controls the collaborator, which makes the unit testable in isolation.

request: What causes a serverless cold start?
a: A new container has to boot and initialise the runtime before it can serve.
b: The platform spins up fresh execution environments when none are warm.

request: Why choose a token bucket over a fixed window?
a: It allows short bursts while still bounding the long-run rate.
b: Fixed windows let double the limit through at a boundary; token buckets do not.

request: What is an N+1 query problem?
a: One query fetches a list, then a query per row fetches its related rows.
b: Loading a collection and then lazily loading each element separately.

request: What should graceful shutdown do?
a: Stop accepting new work, finish what is in flight, then close resources.
b: Drain in-flight requests before tearing down connections and exiting.

request: Why use feature flags?
a: You can turn a change off without a deploy if it goes wrong.
b: They decouple releasing code from enabling behaviour.

request: What is prompt injection?
a: Untrusted input that the model reads as instructions rather than as data.
b: An attacker embedding directives in content the model later treats as its own prompt.

request: Name a limitation of RAG.
a: If retrieval misses the relevant chunk, the model has nothing to ground on.
b: Answer quality is capped by whatever the retriever surfaces.

request: Why is approximate nearest neighbour search used?
a: Exact search over millions of vectors is too slow to serve interactively.
b: Trading a little recall for a large speedup makes vector search practical at scale.

request: What is chaos engineering for?
a: Injecting failures on purpose so you find weaknesses before they find you.
b: Deliberately breaking things in production to validate resilience assumptions.

request: How does a blue-green deploy work?
a: Run two identical environments and switch traffic once the new one is verified.
b: Stand up the new version alongside the old, then cut over at the load balancer.

request: What is the difference between a mock and a stub?
a: A stub returns canned data; a mock also asserts how it was called.
b: Stubs supply answers, mocks verify interactions.

request: How is observability different from monitoring?
a: Monitoring watches known failure modes; observability lets you ask new questions.
b: Monitoring answers questions you predicted; observability handles the ones you did not.

request: Why pool database connections?
a: Opening a connection is expensive, so reusing them cuts per-query overhead.
b: It bounds concurrent connections while avoiding repeated handshake cost.

request: Why must migrations be backward compatible during a rolling deploy?
a: Old and new code run at the same time, so both must understand the schema.
b: During rollout two versions share one database, so neither may break the other.

request: What does HTTP 404 mean?
a: The requested resource was not found on the server.
b: It means the server is down.

request: What is the time complexity of binary search?
a: O(log n), because each comparison halves the remaining range.
b: O(n squared).

request: What does git rebase do?
a: It replays your commits on top of another base, rewriting their hashes.
b: It deletes your branch history permanently.

request: What does the D in ACID stand for?
a: Durability — once committed, a transaction survives a crash.
b: Distribution, meaning the data is spread across nodes.

request: Give one difference between TCP and UDP.
a: TCP guarantees ordered delivery and retransmits losses; UDP does neither.
b: TCP is for websites and UDP is for email.

request: What is the average lookup cost in a hash map?
a: Constant time on average, degrading toward linear as collisions rise.
b: It is always exactly one operation, with no exceptions.

request: What does TLS provide?
a: Encryption in transit plus server authentication via certificates.
b: It compresses the data to make pages load faster.

request: What does a garbage collector do?
a: Reclaims memory that is no longer reachable from the program.
b: It defragments the hard drive on a schedule.

request: Is HTTP GET idempotent?
a: Yes — repeating it should not change server state.
b: No, every GET creates a new record.

request: What is a race condition?
a: Behaviour that depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations.
b: When a program runs too fast for the CPU to keep up.
